title: Fractal dimensions of paths on three-dimensional random-walk traces
authors: Qiyuan Shi, Xinyi Li, Youjin Deng
abstract: We study four paths that join the starting site to the final position of a simple random walk of \(N=L^2\) steps on the infinite cubic lattice. The paths are selected on the walk trace---the graph of visited sites and traversed bonds---by different rules: the undirected shortest path \(S_1\), the directed shortest path \(S_2\), the time-respecting shortest path \(S_3\), and the depth \(D_e\) of the final site in a depth-first-search tree. Monte Carlo simulations for \(L\) up to 32768 give mean lengths scaling as \(L^{d_O}\), with \(d_{S_1}=1.48005(9)\), \(d_{S_2}=1.49868(5)\), \(d_{S_3}=1.51205(5)\), and \(d_{D_e}=1.7099(7)\), so that \(d_{S_1}<d_{S_2}<d_{S_3}<d_{\rm LE}<d_{D_e}\), where $d_{\rm LE}=1.62400(5)$ is the known loop-erased-random-walk exponent. Imposing traversal directions increases the shortest-path exponent, and imposing time order increases it further; these constraints therefore change the scaling exponent, not only the amplitude. For every path, the standard deviation scales with the same exponent as the mean, so it is scale-invariant, unlike the visited-site mass; the rescaled length distributions collapse onto a finite-width scaling function. No analytical theory currently predicts these exponents; our results provide precise numerical benchmarks for future studies of path geometry on random-walk traces.
summary: This paper numerically determines the fractal dimensions of several distinct paths traced on the history of a random walk in 3D. By comparing paths defined by different constraints—such as shortest distance versus time-respecting order—the authors show that these constraints lead to measurably different scaling exponents. The results provide precise benchmarks for understanding path geometry in disordered or constrained random systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the fractal dimensions of various paths connecting the start and end points of a simple random walk on an infinite cubic lattice.
main_result: The fractal dimensions for different path selection rules (e.g., undirected shortest path vs. DFS path) are distinct and scale according to specific exponents, providing numerical benchmarks for path geometry.
method: Monte Carlo simulations are used to calculate the mean lengths and analyze the scaling behavior of different path types over large lattice sizes.
model_or_system: The system is a simple random walk on the infinite cubic lattice (Z^3). Paths are defined on the graph formed by the visited sites and traversed bonds of this walk.
key_observables: Mean path lengths ($S_1, S_2, S_3, D_e$), fractal dimensions ($d_O$), and the scaling exponents governing the tails of the path length probability distributions.
important_parameters: The lattice dimension (d=3), the number of steps ($N=L^2$), and the specific path selection rules (undirected shortest, time-respecting, DFS).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a finite-size scaling ansatz for the path lengths and analyzes the algebraic and stretched exponential decay of the distribution tails.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic comparisons of different paths (e.g., for a 16-step walk) and show the scaling collapse of path-length probability densities for various path types.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares path lengths derived from different rules ($S_1, S_2, S_3, D_e$) against known benchmarks (LERW). It then analyzes the scaling of the mean lengths, fluctuations, and the functional form of the path length probability distributions.
why_interesting: While focused on classical random walks, the study of path geometry and scaling exponents in complex, constrained random processes shares mathematical techniques with analyzing entanglement structures or path integrals in quantum field theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of paths constructed from a 16-step random walk on the cubic lattice. (a) One realization of the walk. The number t identifies the site Xt occupied at step t, for t = 0, . . . , 16. Each distinct site is labeled by its first-visit time, and an attached smaller circle records a later visit to the same site. The walk starts at the circle labeled 0. Its final position at t = 16 is the site first visited at t = 6, which is marked by a square and joined to the attached circle labeled 16. The walk visits M = 14 distinct sites. Panels (b)–(f) are constructed from the walk in panel (a). In panels (b), (c), (e), and (f), each site is identified by its first-visit time....

FIG. 2. Mean mass and mean path lengths of 3D random walks against the diffusive length L. Open symbols are Monte Carlo data. Error bars are smaller than the symbol sizes in both main panels. (a) The mass M and the exact asymptote pL2 (solid line), where p is the escape probability. The inset shows M/L2 −p, and the solid line is proportional to L−1. (b) The mean path lengths S1, S2, S3, and De. The solid lines have slopes given by the exponents dO in Table I. The inset shows the ratios S2/S1 and S3/S2 on a logarithmic L axis, and the solid lines are proportional to LdS2 −dS1 and LdS3 −dS2 .

FIG. 3. Fluctuations χO, Eq. (4), of the mass and the path lengths. Open symbols are Monte Carlo data. Error bars are smaller than the symbol sizes in both main panels. (a) The mass fluctuation χM on a logarithmic horizontal axis. The solid line is AM ln L + B, with the exact coefficient AM of Eq. (6) and the constant B from a fit to Eq. (7). The inset shows the remaining correction ∆χM = χM −A ln L −B. The solid line indicates its L−1 decay. (b) The path-length fluctuations χS1, χS2, χS3, and χDe. The solid lines are power laws with the exponents dχO in Table I.

FIG. 4. Distributions of the mass for L = 2048, 4096, and 8192. (a) Cumulative distribution FL(m) of m = M/L2. The vertical dashed line marks the escape probability p. (b) Probability density fL(z) of the standardized mass z = (M− M)/σM. The dashed curve is the standard Gaussian density.

FIG. 5. Scaling collapse of the path-length probability densities for L = 2048, 4096, and 8192. Panels (a)–(d) show S1, S2, S3, and De, respectively. The densities are plotted as LdOPO,L(ℓ) against ℓ/LdO, as in Eq. (12), where ℓis the path length and dO is taken from Table I.
